newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - G7 undercurrents to drag on debt.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - G7 undercurrents to drag on debt.

text.p: Bond markets are in good shape now, but the medium term outlook is less enticing as the burden of inflation adjustment once again falls to interest rates and currencies take a back seat, analysts said on Monday.
The Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations on Saturday said major misalignments in exchange markets in April 1995 had been corrected. But analysts said that may not reign in the dollar.
"The interest rate implication from the G7 meeting is that the Fed may postpone an interest rate increase if the dollar remains strong," said Neil Mackinnon of Citibank in London.
"Defensive trading characterises the activity we are seeing at the moment," said Mackinnon, chief economist at Citibank.

If the Federal Reserve did delay raising U.S. interest rates and that was factored into the market, he said it could produce a window of opportunity for bonds but the economic outlook in the U.S. was not favourable.

"Generally speaking the economic data out of the U.S. is pretty robust and there are still concerns about the impact of the tight labour market on wage inflation, so it is difficult to get too enthusiastic about the bond markets over the near term."
Others said the G7 would keep current market trends intact.

"They took the guns out of the holsters but they have yet to load and aim them. There is not much inspiration for the market," said Kirit Shah, chief market strategist at Sanwa International in London.
"If anything I'm slightly bearish rather than bullish because there was no specific comment on interventions or levels."

Shah said the dollar might slip a little but would then regain the upside targeting of 1.70 marks, 127/130 yen in the medium term, before correcting again. At 1217 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1.6530/32 marks and 122.49/122.59 yen.

He said there was slightly more bias to the downside than the upside for bonds at current levels. He saw the 10-year T-note/Bund yield spread widening to 100 basis points. The gap is now 90 basis points, up from 54 at the start of the year.
Mackinnon was also unenthusiastic aobut European bond markets, Trading activity for this session was positive, but bonds were running out of space to the upside.

He said German Bund futures were likely to stall at around 103.00 and in Britain, although there was also some repreive from higher interest rates on the political front, gilts could still run out of steam.
March Bund futures were at 102.61, up 0.07 on the day.
"The markets will be looking at the Bank of England inflation report, where no doubt the Bank will be pressing for an interest rate increase. So that could knock the gilt market," Mackinnon said.
British gilts were trading at a spread of 166 basis points against Bunds, compared with 190 in early January.
Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase in London, said overall the G7 communique was reasonably financial market friendly when compared with the Plaza accord in 1985 and the Louvre accord in 1987.
"Then, they were prepared to take very strong action in the way of huge intervention and supporting interest rate moves to correct the misalignment of currencies, Marshall said.
"But this time around they feel the currencies aren't far off being fairly valued...and therefore they don't need to take dramatic action to correct it," he said.
But, he said the risk was the market might not see the G7 statement as going far enough to stop the dollar moving higher.
"They will test the G7's resolve to see what they are prepared to do to stablise the currency and actions will speak larger than words," Marshall said.
